final_proof:
The claim as stated is false, because there is no assumption that f is surjective. For example, let T₁ be a one-point space, let T₂ = ℚ with its usual topology, and let f:T₁→ℚ be the constant map with value 0. The space T₁ is compact and locally connected, ℚ is Hausdorff, and f is continuous. On the other hand, ℚ is not locally connected. Indeed, if a subset A of ℚ contains two distinct points a<b, choose an irrational number r with a<r<b. Then A∩(−∞,r) and A∩(r,∞) are disjoint, nonempty sets open in A whose union is A, so they separate A. Thus the only connected subsets of ℚ are singletons. Since no singleton is open in ℚ, no point of ℚ has a connected open neighborhood. Hence ℚ is not locally connected.

The natural corrected statement, stronger than merely adding surjectivity, is this: the image f(S₁), with the subspace topology inherited from T₂, is locally connected. In particular, if f is surjective, then T₂ is locally connected.

We first prove a general lemma.

Lemma. If q:X→Y is a quotient map and X is locally connected, then Y is locally connected.

Proof. Let U be an arbitrary open subset of Y. The components of the open subspace q⁻¹(U) are open in q⁻¹(U), and hence in X. Indeed, if C is such a component and x∈C, local connectedness gives a connected open neighborhood Vₓ of x contained in q⁻¹(U). Because Vₓ is connected and meets C, maximality of the component C gives Vₓ⊆C. Therefore C is the union of the sets Vₓ for x∈C and is open.

On the set of components of q⁻¹(U), let ≈ be the equivalence relation generated by the relation

    C R D  if and only if  q(C)∩q(D)≠∅.

For an ≈-equivalence class E, set Z_E = ⋃_{C∈E} C. This set is open in q⁻¹(U). It is also saturated for the restricted map q_U:q⁻¹(U)→U. In fact, if x∈Z_E, x′∈q⁻¹(U), and q(x′)=q(x), then the components containing x and x′ have intersecting images; hence those components belong to the same equivalence class E, and x′∈Z_E.

The restricted map q_U is itself a quotient map: for B⊆U, the set q_U⁻¹(B)=q⁻¹(B) is open in q⁻¹(U) exactly when it is open in X (because q⁻¹(U) is open), and the quotient property of q then says exactly that B is open in Y, equivalently open in U. Since Z_E is open and saturated,

    q_U⁻¹(q(Z_E)) = Z_E,

so q(Z_E) is open in U, and therefore open in Y because U is open.

Moreover, q(Z_E) is connected. Fix C₀∈E. For every C∈E, the definition of the generated equivalence relation supplies a finite chain C₀,C₁,…,Cₙ=C such that q(Cᵢ)∩q(Cᵢ₊₁)≠∅ for every i. Each q(Cᵢ) is connected, being the continuous image of the connected set Cᵢ, and consecutive members intersect. Hence ⋃_{i=0}^n q(Cᵢ) is connected. All such finite-chain unions contain q(C₀), so their union is connected; that union is precisely q(Z_E).

Every y∈U lies in one of the connected open sets q(Z_E), each of which is contained in U. Thus every point of every open set U has a connected open neighborhood contained in U. This proves that Y is locally connected. ∎

Now put Y=f(S₁), with the subspace topology inherited from T₂, and regard f as a continuous surjection S₁→Y. This map is a quotient map. To see this, let A be closed in S₁. Because S₁ is compact, A is compact. Its continuous image f(A) is compact; and because T₂ is Hausdorff, f(A) is closed in T₂, hence also closed in the subspace Y. Thus f:S₁→Y is a closed continuous surjection. Every closed continuous surjection is a quotient map: if B⊆Y and f⁻¹(B) is closed, then B=f(f⁻¹(B)) is closed, so the quotient criterion holds (equivalently, apply this to complements for the open-set criterion).

The lemma now shows that Y=f(S₁) is locally connected. If f is surjective onto S₂, then Y=S₂, so T₂ is locally connected. This proves the corrected claim and explains precisely why the original statement requires an additional condition such as surjectivity.
